samples.text:
Set Up Pre-commit Hooks That Your Team Will Not Disable

Prerequisites: Python 3.9+ available for the pre-commit tool, and a Git repository.

Step 1 — Install

    python -m pip install pre-commit

Step 2 — Create the config

Create .pre-commit-config.yaml at the repository root:

    repos:
      - repo: https://github.com/pre-commit/pre-commit-hooks
        rev: v5.0.0
        hooks:
          - id: trailing-whitespace
          - id: end-of-file-fixer
          - id: check-merge-conflict
          - id: check-added-large-files
            args: ['--maxkb=500']
      - repo: https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff-pre-commit
        rev: v0.7.0
        hooks:
          - id: ruff
            args: [--fix]
          - id: ruff-format

Pin every rev to a tag, not to a branch. An unpinned hook means a third party can change what runs on every developer's machine without a commit in your repository.

Step 3 — Install the Git hook

    pre-commit install

Step 4 — Run once against everything

    pre-commit run --all-files

This will produce a large diff the first time. Commit it on its own, with a message saying it is a formatting-only change, and add the commit hash to .git-blame-ignore-revs so it does not pollute blame:

    echo "$(git rev-parse HEAD)" >> .git-blame-ignore-revs
    git config blame.ignoreRevsFile .git-blame-ignore-revs

Step 5 — Enforce in CI too

Hooks are local and can be skipped with --no-verify, which is fine and occasionally necessary. Run the same config in CI so nothing lands unformatted:

    - run: pip install pre-commit && pre-commit run --all-files --show-diff-on-failure

Keeping hooks fast is what makes them survive

The rule that matters: the hook set must run in under about three seconds on a typical commit. Anything slower and people will start using --no-verify habitually, at which point you have a CI check and no hook. Put the type checker and the test suite in CI, not in the hook.

Troubleshooting

Hook fails with "executable not found" on a colleague's machine. pre-commit manages its own environments; ask them to run pre-commit clean and try again.

Hooks do not run at all. The install step writes .git/hooks/pre-commit; if another tool overwrote it, re-run pre-commit install.

The formatter and the linter fight each other, each undoing the other's change. Order matters — put the linter with --fix before the formatter.

samples.text:
Shrink a Docker Image With a Multi-Stage Build

Starting point: a single-stage image weighing 1.2 GB. Target: under 100 MB.

Prerequisites: Docker 24+ and a compiled-language project. This example uses Go, but the shape applies to Rust, Java, and any language with a build step.

Step 1 — Look at what is actually in the image

    docker history myapp:latest --no-trunc --format '{{.Size}}\t{{.CreatedBy}}'

Read this before optimizing. In our case the compiler toolchain accounted for 900 MB of the 1.2 GB, which tells you what to do.

Step 2 — Split build from runtime

    FROM golang:1.23 AS build
    WORKDIR /src
    COPY go.mod go.sum ./
    RUN go mod download
    COPY . .
    RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -ldflags="-s -w" -o /out/app ./cmd/app

    FROM gcr.io/distroless/static-debian12
    COPY --from=build /out/app /app
    USER nonroot:nonroot
    ENTRYPOINT ["/app"]

Three things are doing the work here. CGO_ENABLED=0 produces a static binary so the runtime stage needs no libc. The -s -w linker flags strip the symbol table and DWARF data. The distroless base contains no shell and no package manager.

Step 3 — Order layers for cache hits

Notice that go.mod and go.sum are copied and downloaded before the rest of the source. A change to any source file then reuses the dependency layer. Copying everything first means every source edit re-downloads every dependency.

Step 4 — Add a .dockerignore

    .git
    node_modules
    *.md
    dist/
    .env

Without this, the build context includes your entire Git history, which is often the largest thing you send to the daemon.

Step 5 — Build and measure

    docker build -t myapp:slim .
    docker images myapp --format '{{.Tag}}\t{{.Size}}'

Troubleshooting

Binary exits immediately with "no such file or directory" and the file clearly exists. The binary is dynamically linked and the runtime stage has no linker. Set CGO_ENABLED=0, or use a base image with libc.

You need to debug inside the container but there is no shell. That is the point of distroless. Use a debug variant of the base image temporarily, or attach an ephemeral debug container.

TLS calls fail with a certificate error. Distroless static includes CA certificates, but a scratch base does not. Copy /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt from the build stage.

Timestamps break your cache on every build. Use a build argument for anything that changes per build and put it in the last layer.

samples.text:
Deploy a Stateless Service to Kubernetes With Health Probes

Prerequisites: kubectl configured against a cluster, a container image pushed to a registry the cluster can pull from, and a namespace you can write to.

Step 1 — Create the namespace

    kubectl create namespace demo

Step 2 — Write the Deployment

Create deploy.yaml:

    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    metadata:
      name: api
      namespace: demo
    spec:
      replicas: 3
      selector:
        matchLabels: { app: api }
      template:
        metadata:
          labels: { app: api }
        spec:
          containers:
            - name: api
              image: registry.example.com/team/api:1.4.2
              ports:
                - containerPort: 8080
              env:
                - name: LOG_LEVEL
                  value: info
              resources:
                requests: { cpu: 100m, memory: 128Mi }
                limits:   { memory: 256Mi }
              readinessProbe:
                httpGet: { path: /readyz, port: 8080 }
                periodSeconds: 5
              livenessProbe:
                httpGet: { path: /livez, port: 8080 }
                periodSeconds: 10
                failureThreshold: 3

Pin the image to a tag or digest, never latest — a rolling restart with latest can silently pull a different build.

Set a memory limit but consider omitting the CPU limit. CPU is compressible; a limit throttles rather than protects, and CPU throttling is a very common cause of mysterious latency.

Make readyz and livez different. Readiness should check that the process can serve traffic, including dependencies. Liveness should only check that the process is not wedged — if liveness checks a database, a database blip restarts every pod at once.

Step 3 — Expose it

    apiVersion: v1
    kind: Service
    metadata:
      name: api
      namespace: demo
    spec:
      selector: { app: api }
      ports:
        - port: 80
          targetPort: 8080

Step 4 — Apply and watch

    kubectl apply -f deploy.yaml
    kubectl -n demo rollout status deployment/api --timeout=120s

Step 5 — Verify from inside the cluster

    kubectl -n demo run curl --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl --restart=Never -- \
      curl -sS http://api.demo.svc.cluster.local/healthz

Troubleshooting

Pods stuck Pending. Usually unschedulable due to resource requests. Run kubectl -n demo describe pod and read the events at the bottom.

CrashLoopBackOff. Get the previous container's logs with kubectl -n demo logs <pod> --previous.

OOMKilled. Your memory limit is below actual usage. Raise it, then find out why usage is what it is.

Service returns no endpoints. The Service selector does not match the pod labels. Check with kubectl -n demo get endpoints api.

samples.text:
Add Sign-In With an OAuth 2.0 Provider Using the Authorization Code Flow

Prerequisites: a registered application with the identity provider, and an HTTPS callback URL. This guide uses the authorization code flow with PKCE, which is the right choice for both web apps and native clients.

Step 1 — Register your redirect URI

In the provider's console, register exactly https://app.example.com/auth/callback. Providers match this string exactly; a trailing slash difference will fail.

Step 2 — Store your client credentials

Set them as environment variables read at startup:

    export OAUTH_CLIENT_ID="client_abc123"
    export OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET_FILE="/run/secrets/oauth_client_secret"
    export OAUTH_ISSUER="https://id.example.com"

Read the secret from a file rather than an environment variable where your platform supports it, so it does not appear in a process listing or a crash dump.

Step 3 — Build the authorization request

Generate a code verifier and challenge per attempt:

    const verifier = base64url(crypto.randomBytes(32));
    const challenge = base64url(crypto.createHash('sha256').update(verifier).digest());

Store the verifier and a random state value in the user's session, then redirect:

    https://id.example.com/authorize
      ?response_type=code
      &client_id=client_abc123
      &redirect_uri=https%3A%2F%2Fapp.example.com%2Fauth%2Fcallback
      &scope=openid%20profile%20email
      &state=<random>
      &code_challenge=<challenge>
      &code_challenge_method=S256

Step 4 — Handle the callback

First compare the returned state to the session value and abort if they differ. This is what prevents a cross-site request forgery on the login endpoint, and it is the step people skip.

Then exchange the code, server side:

    POST https://id.example.com/token
    content-type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

    grant_type=authorization_code&code=<code>&redirect_uri=<same as before>
    &client_id=<id>&client_secret=<secret>&code_verifier=<verifier>

Step 5 — Validate the ID token

Do not trust the token because it arrived over TLS. Verify the signature against the provider's JWKS, and check the issuer, the audience, and the expiry. Use a maintained library; hand-rolled JWT validation is a well-known source of vulnerabilities.

Step 6 — Create your own session

Issue your own session cookie with HttpOnly, Secure, and SameSite=Lax. Do not put the provider's access token in a cookie readable by JavaScript.

Troubleshooting

"redirect_uri_mismatch". The URI in the authorization request and the token request must be byte-identical and both must match what is registered.

"invalid_grant" on exchange. Authorization codes are single-use and short-lived. A double-submitted callback, often from a browser prefetch, will burn the code.

The ID token validates locally but not in staging. Your JWKS cache is stale after a provider key rotation. Respect the cache headers and refresh on an unknown key id.

samples.text:
Structured Logging in Python That Is Actually Queryable

Prerequisites: Python 3.11+ and a log destination that parses JSON.

Step 1 — Stop using print and f-string log messages

A line like log.info(f"user {uid} placed order {oid}") is unqueryable. You cannot filter by uid without a regular expression that will break the first time someone changes the wording.

Step 2 — Configure a JSON formatter

    python -m pip install python-json-logger

Create logging_setup.py:

    import logging, os, sys
    from pythonjsonlogger import jsonlogger

    def configure():
        handler = logging.StreamHandler(sys.stdout)
        handler.setFormatter(jsonlogger.JsonFormatter(
            "%(asctime)s %(levelname)s %(name)s %(message)s",
            rename_fields={"levelname": "level", "asctime": "ts"},
        ))
        root = logging.getLogger()
        root.handlers = [handler]
        root.setLevel(os.environ.get("LOG_LEVEL", "INFO"))

Write to stdout, not a file. In a container, the runtime handles collection; a file inside a container is a file you will lose.

Step 3 — Attach structured fields

    log.info("order placed", extra={"user_id": uid, "order_id": oid, "amount_cents": 4999})

The message becomes a stable string you can group by, and the variables become fields you can filter and aggregate.

Step 4 — Add request context automatically

Use a context variable and a filter so every log line inside a request carries the request id without every call site passing it:

    import contextvars
    request_id = contextvars.ContextVar("request_id", default=None)

    class ContextFilter(logging.Filter):
        def filter(self, record):
            record.request_id = request_id.get()
            return True

Step 5 — Set the level per environment

    export LOG_LEVEL=DEBUG   # local
    export LOG_LEVEL=INFO    # production

Step 6 — Do not log sensitive fields

Maintain an explicit deny list and redact before formatting: passwords, tokens, full card numbers, and anything covered by your data classification policy. A redaction filter at the handler is more reliable than discipline at every call site.

Troubleshooting

Logs are doubled. A library called basicConfig, adding a second handler to the root logger. Set root.handlers explicitly as shown, after imports.

JSON lines are wrapped in another JSON envelope by your collector, so fields are not indexed. Configure the collector to parse the message body as JSON.

DEBUG logs never appear even with LOG_LEVEL=DEBUG. A specific logger has its own level set higher than the root, or a handler has its own level.

Multiline tracebacks break parsing. Configure the formatter to include the traceback as a single string field rather than raw newlines.

samples.text:
Rebase a Long-Running Branch Without Losing Your Mind

Situation: your feature branch is 40 commits behind main and has conflicts. This walks through cleaning it up safely.

Prerequisites: Git 2.40+, and a branch you have pushed somewhere so you have a remote copy to fall back on.

Step 0 — Make a safety branch

    git branch backup/my-feature-before-rebase

This costs nothing and is the difference between an annoying afternoon and a lost week.

Step 1 — Update your view of the remote

    git fetch origin

Step 2 — Squash your own noise first

If your branch has twelve commits of which nine are "fix typo", clean them up before rebasing so you resolve each conflict once instead of nine times:

    git rebase -i origin/main --keep-base

Mark the noise commits as fixup. Note that the interactive flag will not work in an environment without an editor, so run this in your terminal.

Step 3 — Rebase onto main

    git rebase origin/main

Step 4 — Resolve conflicts one commit at a time

For each conflict, edit the files, then:

    git add <resolved files>
    git rebase --continue

If you get lost at any point:

    git rebase --abort

That returns you exactly to where you started. It always works, and it is the reason rebasing is less dangerous than its reputation.

Step 5 — Turn on rerere so you only solve each conflict once

    git config --global rerere.enabled true

If you rebase the same branch repeatedly, this replays your previous resolutions automatically. It is the single most underused Git setting.

Step 6 — Push the rewritten branch

    git push --force-with-lease

Use --force-with-lease, never plain --force. The lease version refuses to overwrite the remote if someone else pushed to your branch since your last fetch.

Step 7 — Clean up

    git branch -D backup/my-feature-before-rebase

Troubleshooting

"fatal: It seems that there is already a rebase-merge directory". A previous rebase was interrupted. Either --continue it or --abort it.

A conflict in a file you never touched. Someone moved or renamed it on main. Check with git log --follow on that path.

--force-with-lease is rejected. Someone pushed to your branch. Fetch and look before you force anything.

After rebasing, your PR shows every commit as changed. That is expected — rebasing rewrites commit hashes.
